newsitem.title: PERU: Peru sends Boeing "black boxes" to United States.
newsitem.headline: Peru sends Boeing "black boxes" to United States.

text.p: Aeroperu said on Sunday it was sending two "black box" flight recorders, recovered from the wreckage of its Boeing 757 that crashed 19 days ago, killing 70 people, to the United States for investigation.
The recorders were found, along with nine more bodies, during weekend rescue operations more than 475 feet (200 meters) below the Pacific Ocean offshore northwest of Lima.

Aeroperu officials said the boxes, with vital clues as to what made the Boeing plunge into the sea in the foggy, early hours of Oct. 2, would be sent to the National Transporation Safety Board in Washington.
Rescuers were waiting for optimum conditions to bring up the bodies.
Prior to this weekend's joint underwater operation by Peru's navy, Aeroperu and U.S. firm Oceaneering Technologies, only 14 bodies had been found floating in the ocean in the days after the crash.

The Peruvian government has pinned the blame for the accident on technical faults that made the computers aboard the plane "go crazy," leaving pilot Eric Schreiber without instruments as he struggled to return to Lima after taking off for the Chilean capital of Santiago.
But investigators from Aeroperu, Boeing, engine maker Pratt & Whitney, the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration and the National Transporation Safety Board, have so far reserved judgment.
The 70 dead -- 61 passengers and nine crew members -- were from Chile, Peru, Mexico, Ecuador, the United States, Italy, Great Britain, New Zealand, Spain, Colombia and Venezuela.

The accident, one of the worst in Peru's aviation history, came seven months after a Boeing 737 belonging to local Faucett airline crashed and killed all 123 people on board near Peru's second city, Arequipa. Since 1967, a total of 601 people have been killed in air crashes in Peru.
